judge: solution_ok is False — Rejected on solution_ok only. The key (qualitative categorical) is correct in all three instances, and each key letter points to the right option text. All three distractors carry a tag, are definitely wrong, and fit their tagged error. The 4-distinct-answers count is right in g003 (rabbit, dog, hamster, fish), g005 and g007 (Vodacom or Cell C, MTN, Telkom and the third provider).

The flaw is in step 2 of every worked solution. It says 'Only 4 different answers appear among the five responses, and some learners gave the same answer, so every response comes from a limited set of possibilities.' That is a non sequitur. Any five responses have at most five distinct values, and repeats in a small sample do not show that the set of possible answers is limited. The same reasoning would call a set of free-text opinions categorical as soon as two learners repeated a phrase. A child would learn 'repeated answers mean categorical', which is false.

The book's criterion for categorical data is that the question itself allows only a limited set of possible responses. The solution should justify this from the question: there are only a few cellular providers to choose from, or a learner picks a kind of pet from a small set of common pets. It should not count distinct values in the sample.

The pet stem (g003) is the weaker one. The question gives no explicit limited set, so the explanation has to state the assumption that pets fall into a small number of kinds. Rewrite step 2 (and step 4 if it echoes the sample-count reasoning) in all three instances and the family can pass. Options and key need no change.

misconceptions.label: Calls a count continuous
misconceptions.description: The student sees a data set of counts written as whole numbers (messages sent, sweets in a packet, questions answered correctly) and calls it continuous, instead of checking whether each value is a count written as an integer.

misconceptions.label: Calls a measurement discrete
misconceptions.description: The student sees a data set of measurements written as decimals (heights such as 1.70 m) and calls it discrete, perhaps because it is a short list of separate values, instead of noticing that the values are measurements that cannot be represented by integers.

misconceptions.label: Calls a set of numbers qualitative
misconceptions.description: The student treats a data set made of numbers as qualitative (anecdotal or categorical), reading the numbers as descriptions or group names because they come with a story about people, instead of recognising a set of numbers as quantitative.

misconceptions.label: Calls a set of choices anecdotal because people gave them
misconceptions.description: The student sees that the data comes from what learners say about themselves (their provider, their favourite spread) and calls it anecdotal, taking anecdotal to mean 'personal reports' rather than 'in the form of a story'.

misconceptions.label: Expects removing one value to leave the range unchanged
misconceptions.description: When asked what happens to the range if the smallest or largest value is removed, or when a value that is not typical of the rest is present, the student expects the range to stay the same or hardly change, forgetting that the range is built only from the largest and the smallest values.

misconceptions.label: Takes the line inside the box for an end of the box
misconceptions.description: The student treats the line inside the box as the first or third quartile, instead of seeing that the quartiles are the two ends of the box and the line inside is the median.

misconceptions.label: Takes the line inside the box for the smallest or largest value
misconceptions.description: The student reads a mark in the middle of the plot as the minimum or the maximum, instead of looking to the ends of the whiskers for those two values.

Put this into the mean: $\begin{aligned}7&=\frac{x+38}{6}\\x+38&=7\times 6\\x+38&=42\end{aligned}$
Subtract $38$ from both sides: $\begin{aligned}x&=42-38\\x&=4\end{aligned}$
Check: $\frac{38+4}{6}=\frac{42}{6}=7$, so $x=4$ gives the mean $7$.
